title: Peer review and publishing at eLife, and the eLife Assessment vocabulary

extracted.subtask_short: Rating claim significance and evidence strength separately
extracted.subtask_description: eLife's two-axis rubric rates a paper's findings on significance (importance/novelty) and separately on strength of evidence (how well the data support the claims), using standardized vocabularies published alongside the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength-of-evidence six-point ladder (claim-support axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional: exemplary use of existing approaches that establish new standards for a field. Compelling: evidence that features methods, data, and analyses more rigorous than the current state-of-the-art. Convincing: appropriate and validated methodology in line with current state-of-the-art. Solid: methods, data and analyses broadly support the claims with only minor weaknesses. Incomplete: main claims are only partially supported. Inadequate: methods, data and analyses do not support the primary claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ready-made ordinal target for scoring how well a given piece of evidence/citation supports the claim it is attached to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance axis independent of evidence-strength axis
rubrics_metrics.description: The eLife Assessment rates significance (Landmark/Fundamental/Important/Valuable/Useful) on an axis explicitly independent of the evidence-strength axis - a paper can report a highly significant (landmark) claim that is only 'incomplete'ly supported, and eLife's format lets reviewers say exactly that rather than collapsing both judgments into one accept/reject decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separates 'is this an important claim' from 'is this claim adequately evidenced' - avoids conflating impressiveness of a stated finding with the strength of the evidence actually offered for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether claims and conclusions are justified by the data
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Reviews must 'describe the strengths and weaknesses of the article, and indicate whether the claims and conclusions are justified by the data.' The operative claim-matching question eLife reviewers answer directly and in public: for each major claim in the paper, is it justified by the data presented, partially justified, or not justified?

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreement about claim support is preserved, not collapsed to one verdict
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Where the reviewers disagree with the claims in an article, this is made explicit within the eLife Assessment and the Public Reviews' - disagreement about whether a claim is supported is not resolved into a single up/down verdict; it is preserved and surfaced to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence requests must be tied to a specific major conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, referees were directed to limit revision requests to changes that bear directly on major conclusions; eLife would only require new experiments where the data were essential to support the major conclusions - a request for more evidence had to be tied to a specific claim it would newly support, not a general call for more rigor.
